item.title: QM surfaces and Bianchi modular forms
item.description:
The formulae below are written in TeX. Read this post on the website to see them typeset.

Let $F$ be an imaginary quadratic field. It was recently claimed in the OpenAI slopdrop that elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields are modular. It seems like this proof will probably hold up (at least, a few experts have come out and said it probably will).

There are a few wrinkles when one tries to generalise the usual modularity of elliptic curves over $\Q$ to an imaginary quadratic field. The first is that an elliptic curve $E/F$ can have CM by $F$ itself, in which case the Galois representation splits as a sum of Hecke characters, and the associated Bianchi form will be Eisenstein rather than cuspidal. This is quite a specific degenerate case, though, and if $E$ has CM by any field other than $F$, or no CM at all, we still expect to get a cusp form. The second wrinkle is that, very occasionally, there is no elliptic curve associated to a given cusp form. Instead, the expected geometric object is an abelian surface with quaternionic multiplication: its endomorphism ring is given by an order in a quaternion algebra over $\Q$.

This possibility was first pointed out by Deligne (per Ciaran Schembri's thesis). The first examples were (twists of) base-change forms, found by Cremona.[1] For a while it was unknown whether this could occur for genuine (i.e. non-base-change) Bianchi forms; it was Schembri who found the first examples, three Bianchi forms over $\Q(\sqrt{-3})$ and one over $\Q(\sqrt{-1})$, none of them base change (even up to twist), associated to genuine QM abelian surfaces. This is Theorem 3.3.1 in his thesis / Theorem 1.1 in the associated paper.[2]

The correspondence can be described via the $L$-function. In the elliptic curve case, the expected relationship between form and curve is $L(f,s) = L(E,s)$. When $f$ has an associated QM surface $A$, the correct modularity relationship is $L(f,s)^2 = L(A,s)$.

I have wondered about this phenomenon since the start of my PhD. Early on, I learned about the classical results of Shimura that constructs an elliptic curve from a cusp form $f$ by integrating it over its level group $\Gamma_0(N)$ to get a period lattice $\Lambda_f$; the quotient $\C / \Lambda_f$ is then an elliptic curve $E_f(\C)$, and in particular, a curve modular by $f$. There is no similar method to do this in the imaginary quadratic case; a Bianchi cusp form has realisations as a differential $i$-form for $i=1,2$, and the period lattices associated to both are $1$-dimensional real lattices. They can be smooshed together to get a 2-dimensional lattice in $\C$, but this seems to have no arithmetic meaning. When the Bianchi form $f$ has an associated elliptic curve $E_f$, the period of the $1$-form is (conjecturally) a rational multiple of the covolume of $\Lambda_f$, multiplied by $\sqrt{D}$, for $D$ the discriminant of $F$. This was proved by Trifković[3] in the case of a base-change form, but remains open in general. Just from looking at the modularity relation in the case of $f$ having an associated QM surface $A$, it seems likely that the right statement is that the square of the period of the $1$-form is a multiple of the covolume of the period lattice of $A$, although as far as I am aware this is not written down anywhere.

It does not seem like there is a way to reconstruct $E_f$ from the periods of $f$. I find this funny really, as the Shimura period lattice construction has been around since the 60s, and it took until Wiles et. al. in the 90s/00s to prove that one could go in the other direction. And these curve → form methods seem to be the more robust ones, since nowadays all kinds of theorems about modularity of elliptic curves are known, but very few geometric constructions of period lattices exist. I would be very happy if someone figured out how to do this in the Bianchi case (and have spent a lot of time thinking about it myself).

Somehow, I feel that the generic construction one is after is a QM surface $A$ satisfying $L(f,s)^2 = L(A,s)$ in all cases. It is just that, in the overwhelming majority of cases, the QM surface is $E \times E$, with endomorphism ring $M_2(\Z)$ (a split quaternion algebra). The $L$-function relation is then $L(f,s)^2 = L(E,s)^2$, from which follows the usual one.[4]

This is essentially the content of Conjecture 3 in Taylor's 1994 ICM paper,[5] albeit phrased a little differently. Taylor (and many others) use the name "fake elliptic curve" to describe the QM surface. I don't really care for this name, so I won't use it.

This uniform description is nice, but it does make it clear that the job of building the correct geometric object out of a Bianchi form is even more difficult than it seemed before. In most cases one only needs to construct an elliptic curve, so one requires two complex periods. Both periods seem to be bound up in the period of the $1$-form, and although one could imagine some sufficiently ingenious piece of arithmetic-analytic gymnastics giving a way to "disentangle" these periods, I know of nothing remotely like this actually being possible. Something like this would already be a big boon. But even that is not enough! Because to construct $A$ in the few cases that it is not a square of an elliptic curve, there are two more periods missing, and nowhere obvious to get them from.

Since the associated surface is QM, I would expect you only really need to know the volume of the period lattice (which should be essentially the $1$-period), plus a "direction" vector that generates the whole QM lattice, but again, there seems to be essentially no hope of actually doing this in practice.[6]

Given an individual Bianchi cusp form of level $\mathfrak{n}$, it is possible to find and certify the modularity of an associated elliptic curve, assuming there is one, although the algorithm is a little ignorant, compared to the direct construction of Shimura. One writes down all elliptic curves of conductor $\mathfrak{n}$, checks which one has the right traces of Frobenius, then uses Faltings-Serre-Livné to match the Galois representations. The state-of-the-art in the QM surface case is what Schembri does, which is to write down a Shimura curve associated to the order $\mathcal{O}$ in the suspected quaternion algebra $B$, use a Baba-Granath model to relate points on the curve to surfaces with QM by $\mathcal{O}$, and search for points that give a surface with the right traces of Frobenius. The exact details can be found in Chapter 2 of Schembri's thesis.

At the previous LuCaNT, John Cremona gave a talk on the status of elliptic curve data in the LMFDB, and shared with me afterwards a list of labels of all Bianchi forms currently in the LMFDB with no associated elliptic curve. This list mostly sat on my laptop, gathering dust, until I came back around to thinking about geometrically constructing QM surfaces in June this year. I gave the job of finding geometric objects for all of these to a Claude code, mostly out of curiosity to see if it could actually do it. By this time it had become clear AIs were getting quite good at math, and although it needed the occasional poke towards doing things that seem obvious to you and me,[7] it mostly did a very good job. This is one of the areas it seems that AI is excelling at in math, where the gory details of a complicated computation have been worked out and written down across some number of sources, and the main work is in writing efficient code, organising the data, and computing examples.[8]

Most of the forms have no associated elliptic curve only because the LMFDB doesn't contain data up to that bound, and Claude dilligently found curves in each case. A handful more forms are twists of base-change, and their associated surfaces can be computed by finding the surface associated to the classical form and extending scalars. In the end, there was only one Bianchi form (up to conjugation of the level) associated to a QM abelian surface not arising from base-change, the form with label 2.0.19.1-1849.1-a. Per Claude, writing $a = \frac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}$ and $F = \Q(a)$, the Jacobian of the hyperelliptic curve

$$ C: y^2 = (3 + 5a)x^6 + (68 - 24a)x^5 + (- 148 - 56a )x^4 + (136a - 224)x^3 + (64a + 240)x^2 + (116 -60a )x +( - 20- 12a) $$

is a QM abelian surface over $F$, with QM discriminant $6$, and appears to be modular by 1849.1-a. I say "appears to be" because I haven't gone through the process of proving it using Faltings-Serre-Linvé; this is a service Claude offered, of course, but given I don't really understand how that method actually works (in my head it's just a big magic button that says "prove modularity"), I'd rather not claim an AI proof is correct when I haven't verified it myself.[9] In any case, computing random Euler factors for this curve is pretty convincing to me that the Jacobian of this curve really is the right object.

Claude didn't do anything new to find this curve. Its ability to perform tedious searches is second to none, and it seems to be very adept at all kinds of methods for finding the right parameters on the Baba-Granath curves, which I won't pretend to understand. It did do something I hadn't expected when I gave it the list, which was to filter the forms by their possible QM before searching surfaces. I wasn't aware this was possible, but the arguments it used are quite simple, so I assume they must be munged from some textbook or paper in its training data.

We use the general fact that, if $B$ is a quaternion algebra, $L$ a number field splitting $B$, and $\ell$ is a rational prime such that there is a place $w \mid \ell$ of $L$ with $L_w \simeq \Q_\ell$, then $\ell \nmid D_B$, the discriminant of $B$. The argument goes like this. We have an embedding $L \hookrightarrow \Q_\ell$, and the isomorphism $B \otimes_{\Q} L \simeq M_2(L)$. Tensoring this over $L$ with $\Q_\ell$, we get $(B \otimes_{\Q} L) \otimes_L \Q_{\ell} \simeq B \otimes_{\Q} \Q_\ell$ on the left, and $M_2(\Q_\ell)$ on the right.

The first number field one can plug into this is $L=F$, since $F$ splits $B$.[10] If $\ell$ splits in $F$, the argument tells us that $\ell \nmid D_B$, which cuts the list of possible $B$ down considerably. If $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime of good ordinary reduction for the putative abelian surface $A$, then $L_{\mathfrak{p}} \coloneqq \Q(\sqrt{a_{\mathfrak{p}}^2 - 4N(\mathfrak{p})})$ also splits $B$,[11] and so a prime $\ell$ splitting in any of these fields also cannot divide $D_B$. Running this over the eigenvalues stored in the LMFDB, we are left with possible divisors ${2, 3}$ of $D_B$, so the search is limited to just the quaternion algebra of discriminant $6$. Of course, this is a search over some finite initial set of $\ell$ not split in $F$, and a finite set of Hecke eigenvalues of $f$, but in practice it is enough to narrow down the search space considerably. Once one has a list of possible algebras $B$ that could supply the QM, one can search for a surface. Finding a QM surface where the Euler factors match indicates that it is worth performing a Faltings-Serre-Livné computation, and that supplies the proof that the QM really was the one you suspected from the finite search.

  1. Abelian varieties with extra twist, cusp forms, and elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields. J. London Math. Soc. (2), 45(3):404–416, 1992.
  2. Examples of genuine QM abelian surfaces which are modular, Res. Number Theory (2019) 5:11
  3. Periods of Modular Forms and Imaginary Quadratic Base Change, Canad. Math. Bull. Vol. 53 (3), 2010 pp. 571–576
  4. Editor's note: on rereading this, I believe it should be essentially correct, maybe up to isogeny, in the case where $E$ has no CM. But when $E$ has CM by some other imaginary quadratic field, the endomorphism ring of $E$ is already an order $\mathcal{O}$, so I would expect the endomorphism ring of $E \times E$ to be $M_2(\mathcal{O})$. And this is not going to be a quaternion algebra over $\Q$! I am not sure how to reconcile this.
  5. Representations of Galois Groups Associated to Modular Forms, Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Zurich, Switzerland 1994
  6. The only idea I had that seemed remotely plausible was to compute the period associated to the $2$-form. There is a lot of analogy with the classical case that makes this an attractive idea, but in practice it seems not to help. I am reliably informed by people much cleverer than myself that there are good reasons to expect this period should be associated to regulators of motivic cohomology classes in degree $3$, and for Beillison-type reasons this should not be related to the periods of the underlying curve / surface. I am currently writing a paper about computing $2$-periods, so watch this space (and please don't prompt an AI to do it before I can)
  7. For example, trying to reduce the coefficients defining the elliptic and hyperelliptic curves it was working with, instead of just pig-headedly using models with coefficients in the hundreds of digits
  8. While I was writing this post, Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis. So it would appear that "important and longstanding conjectures" is another area where AIs are excelling at in math.
  9. Although AIs are getting pretty good at basically all math, so whatever Claude would supply if someone asked it is almost certainly going to be right
  10. This follows from considering the endomorphisms of $\mathrm{Lie}(A)$ as an $F$-vector space, and the fact that the QM endomorphisms are all defined over $F$.
  11. This is a more involved calculation, which I would prefer to flesh out another time

item.title: Bianchi Eisenstein series I
item.description:
The formulae below are written in TeX. Read this post on the website to see them typeset.

Let $F$ be an imaginary quadratic field, with ring of integers $\OO_F$. The group $\Gamma = \PSL_2(\OO_F)$ is a Bianchi group. For simplicity, we will assume that the class number of $F$ is 1.[1] We will describe some Eisenstein series for $\Gamma$.

First, a brief recap on Bianchi modular forms. The group $\SL_2(\C)$ acts on $\HH_3 = \C \times \R_{>0}$, the upper half-space, via the following formula:

$$ \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix} \cdot (z,t) = \left( \frac{(az+b)(\overline{cz+d}) +a \overline{c} t^2}{\abs{cz+d}^2 + \abs{ct}^2}, \frac{t}{\abs{cz+d}^2 + \abs{ct}^2}\right).$$

It isn't obvious that this is a group action; it takes a more familiar form when we embed $\HH_3$ into $\Hq$ via $(z,t) \mapsto \tau = z + t\j$:

$$ \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix} \cdot \tau = (a\tau + b)(c \tau + d)^{-1}. $$

This is a multiplication in the non-commuting quaternions, so one should always pick a side upon which to multiply by $(c \tau + d)^{-1}$ and stick to it.[2] A Bianchi modular form of weight $\rho$ for $\Gamma$ is a tuple of functions $f \colon \HH_3 \to \C^n$, satisfying

  1. $f(g \tau) = \rho(J(g,\tau)) f(\tau)$ for all $\tau \in \HH_3$, all $g \in \Gamma$;
  2. $f$ is an eigenvector for the Casimir operators;
  3. $f(\tau)$ is of moderate growth as $t \to 0,\infty$.

Here, $\rho$ is a representation of the maximal compact $\SU(2) \leq \SL_2(\C)$, and $J(g,\tau)$ is the matrix $\bsmallmatrix{cz + d & -ct \\ \overline{c}t & \overline{cz+d}}$.[4]

If you have never thought about a Bianchi modular form before, you can get a long way by mapping these properties onto the three properties defining a classical modular form: automorphy, holomorphicity, and good behaviour at the cusps. In the classical and Bianchi case, all three conditions are the specific versions of the general properties of an automorphic form for a reductive group, specialised to the Lie groups $\SL_2(\R)$ and $\SL_2(\C)$. The essential difference between classical and Bianchi modular forms is that Bianchi forms are almost always vector-valued, rather than scalar-valued. A scalar modular form really is a quirk of the case of $\SL_2(\R)$ rather than the expectation; since its maximal compact $\SO(2)$ is abelian, all of its irreducible representations are characters. Meanwhile $\SU(2)$ is not abelian, and so vector-valued forms really are the "correct" object.

Writing down modular forms is often quite hard and annoying. This is a great advertisement for (clasical) Eisenstein series, which can be very cleanly written down as

$$ G_k(z) = \sum_{(c,d) \in \Z^2}^{\prime} \frac{1}{(cz+d)^k} $$

for $k > 2$ an even integer. Here the primed sum denotes summation excluding the terms that don't make sense, i.e. where $c = d = 0$. We also have the series

$$ E_k(z) = \sum_{g \in \Gamma_{\infty} \backslash \SL_2(\Z)} j(g,z)^{-k} $$

with $\Gamma_{\infty}$ the stabiliser of $\infty$ in $\SL_2(\Z)$, and $j(g,z) = cz+d$ is the usual factor of automorphy. The two series differ by a constant factor of $2\zeta(k)$.

To generalise this to the Bianchi group setting, we will define a very similar factor of automorphy. Define $j(g,\tau) = c \tau + d = cz +d + ct \j$ for $g = \bsmallmatrix{a & b \\c & d}$. There is an additive and multiplicative representation $\sigma$ of $\Hq$ as a (left) $\C$ vector space:

$$ \sigma(z + w\j) = \begin{bmatrix} z & -w \\ \overline{w} & \overline{z} \end{bmatrix} $$

with $J(g,\tau) = \sigma(j(g,\tau))$. Note also that $\sigma(q)^{-1} = N(q)^{-1}\sigma(\overline{q})$. The scalar-valued factor of automorphy $j(g,\tau)$ satisfies the usual cocycle property:

$$ j(gh,\tau) = j(g,h\tau) j(h,\tau). $$

Again, this is multiplication in the quaternions, so the order matters! We can define a "matrix-valued Eisenstein series" by

$$ E_{\rho}^{s}(\tau) = \sum_{g \in \Gamma_{\infty} \backslash \Gamma} \rho(J(g,\tau))^{-1} \left( \frac{t}{N(j(g,\tau))} \right)^s, $$

where $N(\cdot)$ is the quaternion norm, and $\Gamma_{\infty} \leq \Gamma$ is the stabiliser of the cusp $\infty$. The proof that this function is invariant under the action of $\Gamma$ is essentially the same as in the classical case. The factor $\frac{t}{N(j(g,\tau))}$ becomes $\frac{t}{N(j(gh,\tau))}$,[5] and, since $\sigma$ and $\rho$ are both multiplicative, we also have

$$ \rho(J(g,h\tau))^{-1} = \rho(J(h,\tau)) \rho(J(gh,\tau))^{-1}. $$

Then we have

$$ E_{\rho}^{s}(h \tau) = \rho(J(h,\tau)) \sum_{g \in \Gamma_{\infty} \backslash \Gamma} \rho(J(gh,\tau))^{-1} \left( \frac{t}{N(j(gh,\tau))} \right)^s .$$

Assuming the series converges absolutely, we are free to rearrange as we want, and the sum over $gh^{-1} \in \Gamma_{\infty} \backslash \Gamma$ is just a rearrangement.[6] Thus, the whole matrix of functions has the required transformation property.

To get an actual Bianchi modular form from this, it seems sensible to take column of this matrix, which will transform the same way. Assuming moderate growth (which will hold for $s$ in some half-plane), the game is therefore to pick the column with the Casimir eigenvalues we want. Expressions for the Casimir operators acting on vector-valued functions can be found in Friedberg's 1983 On Maass Wave Forms and the Imaginary Quadratic Doi-Naganuma lifting,[7] as Proposition 2.3. To be remotely explicit about this, though, we need to pick a representation. The choice $\rho = \Sym^4$, the symmetric 4th power of the standard representation, is a nice test case where the expressions don't become too unwieldy.

Explicitly, we want to pick out columns of the matrix

$$ \Sym^4(J(g,\tau))^{-1} \left( \frac{t}{N(j(g,\tau))} \right)^s = \frac{t^s}{(r \rbar + s \sbar)^{s+4}} \begin{bmatrix} \rbar^4 & \rbar^3 s & \rbar^2 s^2 & \rbar s^3 & s^4 \\-4 \rbar^3 \sbar & \rbar^2 (r \rbar - 3 s \sbar) & 2 \rbar s (r \rbar - s \sbar) & s^2 (3 r \rbar - s \sbar) & 4 r s^3 \\ 6 \rbar^2 \sbar^2 & 3 \rbar \sbar (-r \rbar + s \sbar) & r^2 \rbar^2 - 4 r \rbar s \sbar + s^2 \sbar^2 & 3 r s (r \rbar - s \sbar) & 6 r^2 s^2 \\ -4 \rbar \sbar^3 & \sbar^2 (3 r \rbar - s \sbar) & 2 r \sbar (-r \rbar + s \sbar) & r^2 (r \rbar - 3 s \sbar) & 4 r^3 s \\ \sbar^4 & -r \sbar^3 & r^2 \sbar^2 & -r^3 \sbar & r^4 \end{bmatrix} $$

with Casimir eigenvalues, where $r = cz+d$ and $s = ct$.[8] Write $e_0,\ldots,e_4$ for the standard unit colums vectors, and write $v_{4}^{i,s}$ for $\Sym^4(J(g,\tau))^{-1} \left( \frac{t}{N(j(g,\tau))} \right)^s e_i$. Then one can show that

$$ \Omega v_{4}^{i,s} = \frac{4 + s - i}{2} \left( \frac{4 + s - i}{2} - 1 \right) v_{4}^{i,s}, \hspace{1pc} \tilde{\Omega} v_{4}^{i,s} = \frac{s+i}{2} \left( \frac{s+i}{2} - 1 \right) v_{4}^{i,s}, $$

with $\Omega$ and $\tilde{\Omega}$ the two Casimir operators defined by Friedberg.[9] This is a rather lengthy and arduous calculation, and I would not really recommend it unless you have a long train journey coming up. We are working with $\Sym^4$, but this can all be done just as easily for $\Sym^n$, and the result is essentially the same, replacing the copies of $4$ with $n$. Absolute convergence then gives us a Bianchi Eisenstein series $E_{n}^{i,s}(\tau)$, defined by

$$ E_{n}^{i,s}(\tau) = E_{\Sym^n}^{s}(\tau) e_i. $$

Of particular interest to number theory are the cohomological Eisenstein series; these are the ones contibuting to the cohomology of $\Gamma$. The usual set of weight representations one is interested in are $V_{k,l} = \Sym^{k} \otimes \overline{\Sym^{l}}$ for integers $k,l \geq 0$, with the bar indicating that the action on the second factor is twisted by complex conjugation. A given Bianchi form shows up in $H^1(\Gamma,V_{k,l})$ if it gives rise to a harmonic differential form valued in $V_{k,l}$. The exact construction is very involved (explained in Section 5.4.3 of Chris Williams' thesis).[10] In the case of $\rho = \Sym^4$, there are exactly three Eisenstein series that contribute to cohomology, given by the vectors $v_{4}^{1,1}$, $v_{4}^{2,1}$ and $v_{4}^{3,1}$, with coefficient representations $V_{2,0}$, $V_{1,1}$ and $V_{0,2}$ respectively.[11]

The middle term contributes to the cohomology in parallel weight, here $(1,1)$. The groups $H^1(\Gamma,V_{k,k})$ are the only ones to contain cusp forms, and the form defined by $v_{4}^{2,1}$ is the base-change of a weight $3$ Eisenstein series. This is an important difference between the classical and Bianchi settings, as forms with trivial nebentype can occur with "odd weight".

The two other columns at $s=1$ also have nice Fourier expansions, but do not contribute to these cohomology groups. Their constant terms also have a different shape to the three cohomological forms. More generally, for the representation $\Sym^n$ with $n$ even, the $i=0$ and $i=n$ columns will give rise to non-cohomological Eisenstein series at $s=1$, and the $i=1$ to $i=n-1$ columns will give rise to forms in cohomology with coefficients in $V_{n-2,0}, \ldots, V_{0,n-2}$.

I got into Bianchi Eisenstein series after giving a talk about my first paper. Someone in the audience[12] asked whether the congruence between the genuine cusp forms in the paper could be seen at the level of the constant term of the actual functions themselves, as opposed to just in cohomology. This is what happens in the classical case, where $691$ appears in the numerator of $\zeta(12)$, realising the mod $691$ congruence of $E_{12}$ and $\Delta$. In the Bianchi case, this would mean a factor of $173$ appearing naturally in the constant term of the Eisenstein series contributing to $V_{10,10}$ over $F = \Q(\sqrt{-11})$. Figuring this out turned out to be a lot more involved than I had expected, but I now believe the answer is "probably not". The constant term of the relevant Eisenstein series[13] is

$$ -\left( \frac{\sqrt{11}}{\pi} \right)^{23} \cdot \frac{22!}{2^{24}} \cdot \zeta_F(12),$$

and there is no obvious appearance of $173$ anywhere. One can factor the zeta value to get $\zeta_F(12) = \zeta(12) L(\chi_F,12)$, which gives the expected $691$ (since the space of forms also contains the base-change of $\Delta$ to $F$), but no copy of $173$ shows up. Maybe there is some natural scaling of the form that would put $173$ into the value $L(\chi_F,12)$, but I don't really expect that to be true. My overall impression after spending a lot of time trying to understand Bianchi modular forms as analytic objects is that classical modular forms are overall much nicer, with the algebraic and analytic structures interacting far more pleasingly than one can expect to happen in general.

Further reading:

  1. On automorphic functions of half-integral weight with application to elliptic curves, Goldfeld-Hoffstein-Patterson. Number Theory Related to Fermat's last Theorem. Progress in Mathematics, Vol. 26. pp 153-193. 1982.
  2. On Maass Wave Forms and the Imaginary Quadratic Doi-Naganuma Lifting, Friedbeg. Math. Ann. 263, pp. 483-508. 1983.
  3. Eisenstein Series over Complex Quadratic Fields When the Class Number Exceeds One, Steyer. Journal of Number Theory 27, pp 223-237. 1987.

  2. As an aside, if one runs through the same computation for a matrix in $\SL_2(\R)$ acting on $\HH_2$, expressed in the coordinates $(x,y)$, one gets essentially the same formula. This is easier, since multiplication in the complex numbers commutes.[3]
  3. As an aside to the aside, I have always enjoyed the comment in Section 2.2.4 of Chris Williams' thesis that introduces this action: "Alternatively, the action can be worked out painfully and explicitly to give [the (z,t) form above]"
  4. This is not strictly in the maximal compact, but this is not actually a problem. One should divide by the square root of its (real) determinant to land in $\SU(2)$, then post-multiply by a power of the determinant on the outside of $\rho$. This is the usual headache created by $\SL$ and $\GL$ automorphic forms. Probably we should be doing everything in terms of a slash action, but there's already too much notation in this post. I believe everything I have written is correct anyway.
  5. this follows from the transformation formula for the $\SL_2(\C)$ action and the cocycle property
  6. This requires a little bit of thought, but it is true.
  7. Math. Ann. 263, pp. 483-508
  8. With apologies to mobile users.
  9. Denoted $\Psi$ and $\tilde{\Psi}$ in his paper.
  10. Overconvergent modular symbols over number fields, PhD thesis, University of Warwick, 2016.
  11. Generally it seems that the $s=1$ Eisenstein series are the most "well-behaved": the Fourier expansion of a Bianchi form is in terms of linear combinations of derivatives of Bessel functions, whereas the $s=1$ forms all have nice expressions in pure Bessel functions only. One must be more careful when dealing with the $s=1$ series at lower weight representations than $\Sym^4$, though. There is a generalisation of the classical real analytic Eisenstein series, a scalar-valued function associated to the trivial representation, but its value at $s=1$ is either not defined, or needs to be defined via analytic continuation (I can't quite remember which). The $s=1$ functions associated to the representation $\Sym^2$ are similarly a little finicky due to lack of absolute convergence, giving an analogue of the classical $G_2$, with its almost-invariance.
  12. either at the Nottingham or London NT seminar, I can't remember which now. Both audiences had lots of useful and interesting things to say!
  13. This is the constant term of the Eisenstein series $G_{23}^{12,1}(\tau)$, which I have not actually defined anywhere. It is the sum over pairs $(c,d)$ in $\OO_F^2$ not equal to $0$, as in the classical case, and is again related to $E_{23}^{12,1}(1,\tau)$ by a factor with a zeta value
